segments.text: On a Sunday afternoon in August 1628, Sweden's newest warship set sail in front of a crowded harbour.

image.file: File:Swedish warship Vasa, sank 1628, Vasamuseet, Stockholm (31) (35872469650).jpg

visual.label: Vasa today, Vasa Museum, Stockholm (photo: Richard Mortel, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: It was meant to be one of the most powerful warships in the Baltic.

image.file: File:Vasa, Swedish warship 1628 (30352310637).jpg

visual.label: Vasa's carved stern and gunports (photo: Sonse, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: It sailed about thirteen hundred metres.

visual.label: the whole of Vasa's only voyage

segments.text: Then a gust of wind pushed it over, water poured in through its open gunports, and within minutes it had sunk.

image.file: File:Vasa - A fully intact 17th century war ship that was salvaged (24228886654).jpg

visual.label: Open gunports on Vasa's hull (photo: Jorge Láscar, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: Today, that same ship stands almost complete in a museum in Stockholm.

image.file: File:"Vasa", a fully intact 64 gun warship from the 17th century that was salvaged (24229632684).jpg

visual.label: Vasa in the Vasa Museum (photo: Jorge Láscar, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: The museum says more than ninety-eight percent of it is original.

visual.label: of the ship is original

segments.text: So how does a brand-new warship sink in sight of its own capital? Why did nobody stop it?

image.file: File:Vasa, Swedish warship 1628 (30352271327).jpg

visual.label: Vasa's stern, Vasa Museum (photo: Sonse, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: And how did it come back from the bottom of the harbour, three hundred and thirty-three years later?

image.file: File:Vasa 24 april 1961 kl 903.jpg

visual.label: Vasa breaks the surface, 24 April 1961 (Vasamuseet, public domain)

segments.text: It all began with an order from the king.
In January 1625, King Gustav the Second Adolf signed a contract for four new warships.

image.file: File:Portret van Gustav II Adolf (1594-1632), koning van Zweden Rijksmuseum SK-A-1723.jpeg

visual.label: Gustav II Adolf, King of Sweden 1611-1632 (Rijksmuseum, public domain)

segments.text: The builders were a Dutch master shipwright, Henrik Hybertsson, and his business partner, Arendt de Groote.

image.file: File:Suecia 1-013 ; Kastellholmen Skeppsholmen 1670.jpg

visual.label: Ships in Stockholm's harbour, engraving by Erik Dahlberg, c. 1670-90 (public domain)

segments.text: There were no blueprints. The king approved the main dimensions, and Henrik shaped the hull with traditional rules of proportion.

image.file: File:Swedish warship Vasa, sank 1628, Vasamuseet, Stockholm (5) (36225483416).jpg

visual.label: Vasa's hull, Vasa Museum (photo: Richard Mortel, CC BY 2.0)
visual.evidence: Vasa Museum audio guide: "there were no blueprints"

segments.text: Thousands of oak trees went into the hull.

image.file: File:Vasa - A fully intact 17th century war ship that was salvaged (24763582591).jpg

visual.label: Oak planking along Vasa's side (photo: Jorge Láscar, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: By the summer of 1626, Henrik was ill. He handed the work to his assistant, Hein Jakobsson, and died the next year.
The finished ship was huge: sixty-nine metres long, and more than fifty metres from keel to masthead.
It carried ten sails, and weighed more than twelve hundred tonnes when fully fitted out.

image.file: File:Vasa rig diagram.jpg

visual.label: Vasa's ten sails (diagram: Fred Hocker, Vasa Museum, CC BY 3.0)

segments.text: It was built for sixty-four guns. Forty-eight of them were bronze twenty-four-pounders, each firing a ten-kilogram shot.

visual.label: bronze 24-pounders, 10 kg shot each

segments.text: And instead of a single gun deck, Vasa carried guns on three decks.

image.file: File:Swedish warship Vasa, sank 1628, Vasamuseet, Stockholm (32) (36099911392).jpg

visual.label: Rows of gunports on Vasa's side (photo: Richard Mortel, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: On top of that came hundreds of carved and painted sculptures.

image.file: File:"Vasa", a fully intact 64 gun warship from the 17th century that was salvaged (24229649544).jpg

visual.label: Copies of Vasa's sculptures painted in reconstructed colours, Vasa Museum (photo: Jorge Láscar, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: Every one of those features added weight. And much of that weight sat high above the water.

image.file: File:Vasa, Swedish warship 1628 (43476315790).jpg

visual.label: Sculptures on Vasa's stern (photo: Sonse, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: Before the ship ever left port, there was a warning.
In the summer of 1628, probably in early July, the captain, Söfring Hansson, arranged a demonstration.

image.file: File:Swedish warship Vasa, sank 1628, Vasamuseet, Stockholm (44) (36099794422).jpg

visual.label: Vasa's upper deck, Vasa Museum (photo: Richard Mortel, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: Watching was Vice Admiral Klas Fleming, deputy to the commander of the Swedish navy.

image.file: File:Klas Fleming, 1592-1644 - Nationalmuseum - 15638.tif

visual.label: Klas Fleming (1592-1644), portrait copy (Nationalmuseum, public domain)

segments.text: Thirty men ran together from one side of the deck to the other, to make the ship roll.

image.file: File:Vasa - A fully intact 17th century war ship that was salvaged (24489442299).jpg

visual.label: Vasa's upper deck and rigging (photo: Jorge Láscar, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: After a few runs, the ship heeled so far they feared it would capsize at the quay. The test was stopped.

visual.label: men running across the deck

segments.text: According to testimony given later, Fleming said: If only His Majesty were at home!

image.file: File:Klas Fleming, 1592-1644 - Nationalmuseum - 15638.tif

segments.text: But the king was at war in Prussia, and he had been pressing for the ship to sail.

image.file: File:Gustav II Adolf SP011.jpg

visual.label: Gustav II Adolf on horseback, engraving by Jakob van Heyden, 1632 (public domain)

segments.text: The danger was never reported to him. Under that pressure, Fleming let the voyage go ahead.

image.file: File:Vasa, Swedish warship 1628 (45291155561).jpg

visual.label: Vasa, Vasa Museum (photo: Sonse, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: Then came the day of the maiden voyage.
On Sunday, the tenth of August 1628, Vasa cast off below the royal palace in Stockholm.

image.file: File:Stockholm karta 1642.jpg

visual.label: Stockholm in 1642, hand-drawn map (public domain)

segments.text: Between one hundred and fifty and two hundred people were on board, including family members and guests.

visual.label: people on board

segments.text: The crew hauled it along the waterfront with anchors, then set four of its ten sails and fired a salute.

image.file: File:Vasa rig diagram.jpg

visual.label: Vasa's sail plan (diagram: Fred Hocker, Vasa Museum, CC BY 3.0)

segments.text: Thousands of people watched from the shore, among them foreign ambassadors.

image.file: File:Suecia 1-013 ; Kastellholmen Skeppsholmen 1670.jpg

visual.label: Stockholm harbour, engraving by Erik Dahlberg, c. 1670-90 (illustration, public domain)

segments.text: Under the high cliffs of Södermalm, the wind was weak, and the ship drifted.

image.file: File:Stockholm karta 1642.jpg

visual.label: Södermalm's shoreline, map of 1642 (public domain)

segments.text: A small gust heeled it over to port. Slowly, it came back upright.

image.file: File:Vasa, Swedish warship 1628 (45241656232).jpg

visual.label: Vasa's bow, Vasa Museum (photo: Sonse, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: Then, at a gap in the cliffs, a much stronger gust hit.

image.file: File:Swedish warship Vasa, sank 1628, Vasamuseet, Stockholm (5) (36225483416).jpg

visual.label: Vasa's hull, Vasa Museum (photo: Richard Mortel, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: Vasa leaned so far that water poured in through the open gunports on the lower gun deck.

image.file: File:Vasa - A fully intact 17th century war ship that was salvaged (24228886654).jpg

visual.label: Gunports with their lids open (photo: Jorge Láscar, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: The captain ordered the sails let loose and the gunports shut. It was too late.

image.file: File:Vasa - A fully intact 17th century war ship that was salvaged (24763582591).jpg

visual.label: Vasa's side, Vasa Museum (photo: Jorge Láscar, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: Within minutes, it sank thirty-two metres to the bottom, with the tops of its masts still above the water.

visual.label: depth of the wreck

segments.text: Some survivors swam about a hundred and twenty metres to the island of Beckholmen. Small boats picked up others.

image.file: File:Stockholm karta 1642.jpg

visual.label: Stockholm's harbour, map of 1642 (public domain)

segments.text: The museum puts the death toll at about thirty. Three letters written at the time give thirty, forty and fifty.

image.file: File:Swedish warship Vasa, sank 1628, Vasamuseet, Stockholm (33) (36225078176).jpg

visual.label: Vasa, Vasa Museum (photo: Richard Mortel, CC BY 2.0)
visual.evidence: Vasa Museum FAQ: exact number unknown

segments.text: Most of the dead were trapped inside the ship.

image.file: File:Swedish warship Vasa, sank 1628, Vasamuseet, Stockholm (28) (35433637284).jpg

visual.label: Vasa's stern, Vasa Museum (photo: Richard Mortel, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: Stockholm wanted to know who was to blame.
The captain was jailed almost at once. He insisted the crew had been sober, and the guns properly secured.

image.file: File:Slottet Tre Kronor 1661.jpg

visual.label: Tre Kronor palace, Stockholm, painting of 1661 (public domain)

segments.text: On the fifth of September, an inquest opened, led by Admiral of the Realm Karl Karlsson Gyllenhielm, the king's half-brother.

image.file: File:Carl Carlsson Gyllenhielm, 1574-1670 (Jacob Heinrich Elbfas) - Nationalmuseum - 15163.tif

visual.label: Karl Karlsson Gyllenhielm, attributed to J. H. Elbfas (Nationalmuseum, public domain)

segments.text: Officer after officer said they knew of no fault. The ballast, a hundred and twenty tonnes of stone, had been loaded as required.

image.file: File:Swedish warship Vasa, sank 1628, Vasamuseet, Stockholm (24) (35872503640).jpg

visual.label: Vasa, Vasa Museum (photo: Richard Mortel, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: The builder, Hein Jakobsson, said he had followed Henrik's design, which the king himself had approved.

image.file: File:Swedish warship Vasa, sank 1628, Vasamuseet, Stockholm (27) (35872487860).jpg

visual.label: Royal coat of arms on Vasa's stern (photo: Richard Mortel, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: But he admitted widening the ship by about forty centimetres, which the museum reads as a sign of doubt.

image.file: File:Swedish warship Vasa, sank 1628, Vasamuseet, Stockholm (8) (35433835024).jpg

visual.label: Vasa's bow, Vasa Museum (photo: Richard Mortel, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: Experts told the inquest the ship lacked enough belly, the hull below the waterline, to carry its tall, heavy upper structure.

image.file: File:Vasa rig diagram.jpg

visual.label: Vasa's profile and rig (diagram: Fred Hocker, CC BY 3.0)

segments.text: In other words, its centre of gravity was too high.

visual.title: WHY VASA CAPSIZED
items: Tall, heavy upper structure and guns
Too little hull below the waterline
A gust heels it; open gunports flood

segments.text: And nobody could have calculated that in advance. The mathematics of ship stability arrived more than a century later.

image.file: File:Vasa, Swedish warship 1628 (30352310637).jpg

visual.label: Vasa's stern, Vasa Museum (photo: Sonse, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: No one was punished. The blame fell on the one man who could not answer back: the designer, already dead.

image.file: File:Swedish warship Vasa, sank 1628, Vasamuseet, Stockholm (29) (36132540741).jpg

visual.label: Carvings on Vasa's stern (photo: Richard Mortel, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: The men who were questioned went on to be promoted.

image.file: File:Klas Fleming, 1592-1644 - Nationalmuseum - 15638.tif

visual.label: Klas Fleming (Nationalmuseum, public domain)

segments.text: The guns, though, were far too valuable to leave behind.
In the 1660s, Albrecht von Treileben and Andreas Peckell went down to the wreck with a diving bell.

image.file: File:Fotothek df tg 0003784 Physik ^ Hydrostatik ^ Druck ^ Glocke.jpg

visual.label: A diving bell, engraving from 1685 (illustration; not the Vasa bell; Deutsche Fotothek, public domain)

segments.text: A diving bell works like an upturned glass pushed into water: air stays trapped inside, and the diver breathes it.

visual.title: HOW A DIVING BELL WORKS
items: Diver stands on a platform below
Breathes the trapped air while working

segments.text: An Italian priest who watched in 1663 noted that after about fifteen minutes, the diver came up shivering with cold.

image.file: File:Fotothek df tg 0003784 Physik ^ Hydrostatik ^ Druck ^ Glocke.jpg

visual.evidence: Vasa Museum audio guide, "The first salvage efforts"

segments.text: Working about thirty metres down, they raised more than fifty cannons. Most were sold abroad.

visual.label: cannons raised in the 1660s

segments.text: In 1920, two brothers even asked permission to blow up wrecks in the harbour and sell the black oak. They were refused.

image.file: File:Swedish warship Vasa, sank 1628, Vasamuseet, Stockholm (8) (35433835024).jpg

visual.label: Vasa's dark oak timbers today (photo: Richard Mortel, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: The man who finally found Vasa was an engineer.
Anders Franzén was a fuel engineer for the Swedish navy who hunted for lost warships in his spare time.

image.file: File:Anders Franzen 1961a.jpg

visual.label: Anders Franzén (1918-1993) at the salvage site, 1961 (Vasamuseet, public domain)

segments.text: He searched the archives for clues, and from 1954 he combed Stockholm's harbour in boats lent by the navy.

image.file: File:Stockholm 1637.jpg

visual.label: Stockholm's harbour, map of 1637 (public domain)

segments.text: On the twenty-fifth of August 1956, the coring device he had designed came up with a plug of black, waterlogged oak.
In early September, navy diver Per Edvin Fälting went down. Feeling his way in the dark, he found a wooden wall with rows of square openings. Gunports.

image.file: File:Swedish warship Vasa, sank 1628, Vasamuseet, Stockholm (32) (36099911392).jpg

visual.label: Rows of gunports on Vasa's side (photo: Richard Mortel, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: Why had it survived? The Baltic's brackish water is too low in salt for shipworm, which destroys wooden wrecks in saltier seas.

image.file: File:Vasa - A fully intact 17th century war ship that was salvaged (24857024405).jpg

visual.label: Vasa's bow, Vasa Museum (photo: Jorge Láscar, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: Finding Vasa was one thing. Lifting it was another.
Ideas ranged from filling the hull with ping-pong balls to freezing it in ice.

image.file: File:VASA. Stockholms ström. 1961 - Vasamuseet - 1-242.tif

visual.label: Salvage work on Vasa's upper deck, 1961 (Vasamuseet, public domain)

segments.text: Instead, between 1957 and 1959, navy divers dug six tunnels through the mud underneath the hull.

image.file: File:VASA. Stockholms ström. 1961 - Vasamuseet - 1-240.tif

visual.label: Salvage work on Vasa, 1961 (Vasamuseet, public domain)

segments.text: Steel cables were threaded through the tunnels and attached to two lifting pontoons, named Oden and Frigg.

visual.title: HOW VASA WAS RAISED
items: Cables to pontoons Oden and Frigg

segments.text: On the twentieth of August 1959, the ship came free of the mud. In eighteen stages, it was moved to shallower water off Kastellholmen.

image.file: File:Stockholm karta 1642.jpg

visual.label: Kastellholmen on a map of 1642 (public domain)

segments.text: Divers then spent another year and a half preparing the hull for the final lift.
On the twenty-fourth of April 1961, at three minutes past nine, the first timbers broke the surface, followed by the carved heads of four warriors.

image.file: File:Vasa 24 april 1961 kl 903.jpg

visual.label: 24 April 1961, 9:03 a.m.: carved heads break the surface (Vasamuseet, public domain)

segments.text: Thousands watched, and Swedish television broadcast it live across Europe.

image.file: File:Vasa Beckholmen 1961.jpg

visual.label: Vasa raised between the pontoons, 24 April 1961 (Vasamuseet, public domain)

segments.text: After three hundred and thirty-three years, Vasa was back in the open air.

visual.label: years under water

segments.text: On the fourth of May, it was towed into a dry dock on Beckholmen, the same island survivors had swum to in 1628.

image.file: File:Vasa 14 maj 1961.jpg

visual.label: Vasa at the Beckholmen dry dock, May 1961 (press photo, public domain)

segments.text: Inside, archaeologists recovered more than thirty thousand objects, more than seven hundred sculptures, and the remains of people who died on board.

image.file: File:VASA. Stockholms ström. 1961 - Vasamuseet - 2-117.tif

visual.label: Archaeologists working inside Vasa's hull, 1961 (Vasamuseet, public domain)

segments.text: But the moment Vasa met the air, a second race began.
Waterlogged oak cracks and shrinks as it dries. So from 1962, the hull was sprayed with polyethylene glycol, a wax that replaces the water in the wood.

image.file: File:VASA. Wasavarvet-Alkärret, Stockholm. 1961 - Vasamuseet - 4-20.tif

visual.label: Under Vasa's hull at the temporary Wasavarvet museum, 1961 (Vasamuseet, public domain)

segments.text: The spraying went on for seventeen years, until 1979. Then the ship was dried slowly, for about another decade.
In 1990, the Vasa Museum opened, built around the ship.

image.file: File:"Vasa", a fully intact 64 gun warship from the 17th century that was salvaged (24490192699).jpg

visual.label: Vasa, with a scale model in front, Vasa Museum (photo: Jorge Láscar, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: Then, after a rainy summer in 2000, yellow and white spots began to appear on the wood.

image.file: File:Swedish warship Vasa, sank 1628, Vasamuseet, Stockholm (9) (36100098552).jpg

visual.label: Vasa's timbers, Vasa Museum (photo: Richard Mortel, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: Researchers found the cause: sulphur. On the seabed, bacteria had produced hydrogen sulphide, which soaked into the timbers.

image.file: File:Vasa - A fully intact 17th century war ship that was salvaged (24763582591).jpg

visual.label: Vasa's hull, Vasa Museum (photo: Jorge Láscar, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: In damp museum air, that sulphur slowly turns into sulphuric acid. And iron from corroded bolts speeds up the reaction.

visual.title: THE HIDDEN THREAT
items: Oxygen and humidity in the museum
Iron from old bolts speeds it up

segments.text: A 2002 study in Nature estimated that the remaining sulphur could produce more than five thousand kilograms of sulphuric acid.

visual.label: of potential sulphuric acid

segments.text: Since 2004, the museum has kept the hall at a steady humidity of about fifty-three percent.

image.file: File:Swedish warship Vasa, sank 1628, Vasamuseet, Stockholm (41) (36266532835).jpg

visual.label: Vasa's rigging in the museum hall (photo: Richard Mortel, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: Between 2011 and 2018, thousands of rusting iron bolts were swapped for corrosion-resistant steel, making the ship about eight tonnes lighter.

image.file: File:Swedish warship Vasa, sank 1628, Vasamuseet, Stockholm (37) (35433603574).jpg

visual.label: Vasa's stern quarter, Vasa Museum (photo: Richard Mortel, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: But the hull is still moving. Measurements taken since 2000 show it settling by about a millimetre a year.

image.file: File:Vasa - A fully intact 17th century war ship that was salvaged (24857024405).jpg

visual.label: Vasa on its old support cradle, 2014 (photo: Jorge Láscar, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: The museum warns that without action, the ship would eventually keel over.

image.file: File:"Vasa", a fully intact 64 gun warship from the 17th century that was salvaged (24229632684).jpg

visual.label: Vasa, Vasa Museum (photo: Jorge Láscar, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: So in April 2024, work began on a new support: twenty-seven steel cradles outside the hull, and later a steel skeleton inside it.

image.file: File:Vasa - A fully intact 17th century war ship that was salvaged (24857024405).jpg

visual.label: The old cradle under Vasa's hull, before the new steel supports (photo: Jorge Láscar, 2014, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: Sensors in the new supports will also help establish the ship's real weight, estimated at eight hundred to twelve hundred tonnes.
The goal is to finish by 2028, four hundred years after its only voyage.
So why did Vasa sink?

image.file: File:Vasa, Swedish warship 1628 (30352271327).jpg

visual.label: Vasa's stern, Vasa Museum (photo: Sonse, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: It was too tall and heavy above the waterline, with too little hull below. And its lower gunports were open when the gust came.

image.file: File:Vasa rig diagram.jpg

visual.label: Vasa's profile and rig (diagram: Fred Hocker, CC BY 3.0)

segments.text: The warning came weeks before the voyage, from thirty men running across a deck. It never reached the king.

image.file: File:Swedish warship Vasa, sank 1628, Vasamuseet, Stockholm (44) (36099794422).jpg

visual.label: Vasa's upper deck (photo: Richard Mortel, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: The same cold, brackish water that swallowed the ship is what kept it whole.

image.file: File:Vasa 24 april 1961 kl 903.jpg

visual.label: Vasa surfaces, 24 April 1961 (Vasamuseet, public domain)

segments.text: In 1628, nobody could calculate whether Vasa would stay upright. Today, engineers measure its every movement to less than a millimetre.

image.file: File:Swedish warship Vasa, sank 1628, Vasamuseet, Stockholm (31) (35872469650).jpg

visual.label: Vasa, Vasa Museum (photo: Richard Mortel, CC BY 2.0)

segments.text: Its first voyage lasted thirteen hundred metres. Its second, the fight to keep it standing, is still going on.

image.file: File:"Vasa", a fully intact 64 gun warship from the 17th century that was salvaged (24229632684).jpg

visual.label: Vasa, Vasa Museum (photo: Jorge Láscar, CC BY 2.0)

title: The Warship That Sank 1,300 Metres Into Its First Voyage: Vasa, 1628
description: On 10 August 1628, the Swedish warship Vasa capsized in Stockholm harbour after sailing about 1,300 metres, weeks after a stability test had shown it was dangerously unstable. This documentary follows the ship from the king's order to the inquest that punished no one, the 1660s diving-bell salvage of its guns, its rediscovery in 1956 and its lift in 1961. It ends with the race that is still going on: sulphuric acid in the wood, thousands of replaced bolts and a new steel support due by the 400th anniversary in 2028. Every figure comes from the Vasa Museum and published research (sources below); where sources disagree, we give the range.
sources: Vasa Museum, "The search for Vasa" and "The salvage": https://www.vasamuseet.se/en/vasa-history/search-for-vasa ; https://www.vasamuseet.se/en/explore/vasa-history/salvage
